title: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT SEX, BREASTS, LUST, ADULTERY, PROSTITUTION, AND BROKEN FAMILIES—AND THE REASON WHY MAY BRING YOU TO YOUR KNEES.
paragraphs: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT SEX, BREASTS, LUST, ADULTERY, PROSTITUTION, AND BROKEN FAMILIES—AND THE REASON WHY MAY BRING YOU TO YOUR KNEES.

The Scriptures expose what religion often tries to hide. But Hebrews 4:12–16 reveals something even more astonishing: the God who sees your deepest secrets is the very God who invites you to come closer.
There are things people will never admit in church.
Not because they don't believe in God.
But because they're terrified of what people might think if they knew the truth.
The married man who worships on Sunday but secretly struggles with pornography.
The woman who smiles during fellowship while carrying the shame of an affair nobody knows about.
The young believer who loves Jesus but keeps falling into sexual temptation and wonders whether God has finally grown tired of forgiving them.
The husband and wife sleeping in the same bed but living like strangers.
The person who was sexually violated and has spent years feeling dirty because of something someone else did to them.
The single mother who still hears the judgment in people's voices.
The former prostitute who wonders whether anyone will ever see her as more than her past.
And the person reading this right now who has never told another living soul what happened behind closed doors.
Some of these people are guilty of choices they need to repent of.
Others are carrying wounds they never deserved.
Some are carrying both.
And that distinction matters enormously to God.
Because the Bible does not treat every broken person as though they committed the same sin.
But it does reveal a Savior who knows every story.
And here is what might surprise you.
The Bible is far more willing to discuss the uncomfortable realities of human sexuality than many Christians are.
It talks about breasts.
It talks about sexual desire.
It talks about prostitution.
It talks about adultery, incest, rape, lust, betrayal, pregnancy outside marriage, and families shattered by human decisions.
It even contains an entire poetic book celebrating the beauty of marital love and physical affection.
Why?
Because God is not embarrassed by the human body He created.
He is not confused by the desires He designed.
And He is certainly not surprised by the ways sin has distorted what He originally declared good.
But there is something even deeper happening in Scripture.
God already knows the part of your story you are most afraid to tell Him.
And Hebrews tells us exactly what happens when that hidden place meets the living Word of God.
Hebrews 4:12 declares:

"For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart." (KJV)
Read that last phrase again.
The thoughts and intents of the heart.
Not merely what you did.
Not merely what someone saw.
Not merely what appeared on the screen.
Not merely what you confessed.
The thoughts.
The intentions.
The motives.
The desires you entertained.
The bitterness you protected.
The secret compromises you justified.
The wounds you covered with a convincing smile.
God's Word reaches beneath the behavior and exposes what is happening in the heart.
The original Greek makes this even more piercing.
Hebrews describes God's Word as ζῶν γὰρ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἐνεργής (zōn gar ho logos tou theou kai energēs).
Literally, "For the word of God is living and active."
The word ἐνεργής (energēs) carries the sense of being active or effective.
This is not a dead religious document sitting quietly on a shelf.
God's Word is living and active, accomplishing His purposes and confronting us with His truth.
And then comes a remarkable expression.
κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων καὶ ἐννοιῶν καρδίας
Kritikos enthymēseōn kai ennoiōn kardias.
A discerner or judge of the heart's thoughts and intentions.
The Greek word kritikos describes the capacity to evaluate or judge.
Scripture does not merely identify what happened.
It confronts why.
And that is where things become uncomfortable.
Because we can sometimes hide our behavior from other people.
But we cannot hide our hearts from God.
A person can delete their browsing history.
They cannot delete God's knowledge of what happened.
A person can conceal an affair.
They cannot conceal it from the One who sees all things.
A person can pretend their marriage is healthy.
God knows about the tears that fall after the lights go out.
And a wounded person can spend decades pretending that the abuse never happened.
But the Lord has never been ignorant of their suffering.
Being fully known by God is terrifying when we want to protect our sin. But it becomes a profound comfort when we realize He also sees the wounds nobody else understands.
That is why Hebrews 4 cannot be reduced to a warning about sexual immorality.
The passage is bigger than that.
It reveals the searching power of God's Word, the impossibility of hiding from His sight, and the astonishing mercy available through Jesus Christ.
Listen to verse 13:
"Neither is there any creature that is not manifest in his sight: but all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do." (KJV)
All things.
Naked.
Opened.
Nothing hidden.
The Greek text says:
πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα
Panta de gymna kai tetrachēlismena.
"All things are naked and exposed."
The word gymna means naked or uncovered.
The unusual word tetrachēlismena conveys being laid bare or exposed.
The precise background of the expression is debated, but its meaning in the passage is unmistakable.
Nothing is concealed from God's sight.
And notice something important.
Hebrews is not using nakedness here to create sexual imagery.
It is describing our complete exposure before the God to whom we must give account.
No costume.
No performance.
No carefully edited testimony.
No religious reputation strong enough to conceal the truth.
Just us.
Before Him.
And perhaps that is exactly what frightens us.
Because many of us have spent our lives trying to control what others know about us.
We show them the wedding photographs.
Not the screaming arguments.
We show them the Bible verses.
Not the private messages.
We show them the ministry involvement.
Not the secret addiction.
We show them the happy family portrait.
Not the child who cries because the house no longer feels safe.
And yet the Bible keeps opening doors that respectable society would rather leave closed.
Consider the very beginning.
Genesis 2:25 says Adam and Eve were both naked and were not ashamed.
Before sin entered the world, nakedness itself was not presented as something evil.
The human body was part of God's good creation.
Then Genesis 3 records humanity's rebellion, and shame enters the story.
Suddenly, the man and woman who once stood unashamed begin covering themselves and hiding from God.
The problem was not that their bodies had suddenly become wicked.
The problem was that sin had fractured their relationship with God, with each other, and even with themselves.
And humanity has been hiding ever since.
Hiding behind success.
Hiding behind pleasure.
Hiding behind religion.
Hiding behind relationships.
Hiding behind another secret encounter that promises comfort but leaves the soul emptier than before.
And still the question of Genesis echoes through the centuries.
"Where art thou?" (Genesis 3:9, KJV)
God was not asking because He had lost Adam.
He was confronting a man who was hiding.
And perhaps that question has followed you into this very moment.
Where are you?
Not geographically.
Spiritually.
Where are you in your marriage?
Where are you in your private life?
Where are you in the struggle you keep promising to surrender?
Where are you in the grief you refuse to speak about?
Where are you in your relationship with Jesus?
Because the God who sees everything is not interested in maintaining the illusion that everything is fine.
He calls us into truth.
And Scripture refuses to pretend that sexuality exists outside that truth.
Read the Song of Songs.
You will discover poetic celebrations of attraction, longing, affection, and the beauty of the beloved.
Song of Songs 4:5 uses the imagery of two young gazelles to describe the woman's breasts.
Song of Songs 7:7–8 also contains intimate poetic language.

These passages belong to ancient Hebrew love poetry. Their imagery should be understood within the book's literary and cultural setting rather than treated as a modern anatomical description or a license for voyeurism.
But their presence in Scripture still teaches something important.
The Bible does not teach that sexual attraction within God's design is inherently filthy.
The Hebrew word דּוֹדִים (dodim) can refer to expressions of love or lovemaking, depending on context.
And the Song celebrates the delight of love without pretending that physical affection is absent from human relationships.
The God who created marriage did not accidentally create desire.
Genesis 2:24 presents the union of husband and wife as becoming "one flesh."
Sexual intimacy within marriage is not something Christians need to describe as shameful in order to defend holiness.
It is a good gift that requires faithfulness, mutual honor, and love.
But the same Bible that celebrates marital intimacy also confronts sexual sin.
Jesus makes that unmistakable.
In Matthew 5:27–28, He moves beyond the outward act of adultery and confronts lustful intention in the heart.
He does not condemn the mere recognition that another person is attractive.
He confronts the deliberate cultivation of desire that treats someone as an object of illicit sexual possession.
And that distinction matters.
Because temptation itself is not identical to surrendering to temptation.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
The issue is not whether a person ever experiences an unwanted thought or attraction.
The issue is what they choose to welcome, nurture, pursue, and obey.
God does not call us to pretend we have no bodies.
He calls us to honor Him with them.
And the consequences of refusing that call can be devastating.
Think about David.
A king.
A worshiper.
A man who knew the language of prayer.
Yet 2 Samuel 11 records his adultery with Bathsheba and the terrible abuse of royal power that followed.
Bathsheba was summoned by the king, and the text does not give us grounds to assume she enjoyed equal power or freedom in that encounter.
David then arranged for her husband Uriah to be placed in a deadly military situation.
The biblical account does not romanticize David's actions.
It exposes them.
And when the prophet Nathan confronts him, the king finally says:
"I have sinned against the LORD." (2 Samuel 12:13, KJV)
No more pretending.
No more manipulating appearances.
No more hiding behind a crown.
David's repentance did not erase the harm or the consequences of what he had done.
But it marked a necessary turning toward the God he had offended.
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a broken man pleading for mercy.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me." (Psalm 51:10, KJV)
The Hebrew is beautiful and searching.
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
"Create for me a clean heart, O God."
The verb bera comes from בָּרָא (bara), "to create."
David does not merely ask God to help him manage his reputation.
He asks for inward renewal.
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us have avoided.
We want God to remove the consequences.
But we hesitate to ask Him to transform the desires that led us there.
We want peace without confession.
Healing without honesty.
Forgiveness without repentance.
Restoration without change.
Yet biblical grace is not permission to keep destroying ourselves and others.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy that receives repentant sinners and begins transforming the very lives sin has damaged.
And the Bible makes this clear through stories that many religious communities would rather soften.
Rahab was identified as a prostitute.
Yet Joshua 2 records her response of faith in the God of Israel, and Hebrews 11:31 remembers her among those who acted by faith.
Matthew 1:5 even places Rahab in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
A woman remembered for prostitution appears in the family history of the Messiah.
Not because prostitution was righteous.
Not because her past did not matter.
But because her past did not have the final word over her future.
And then there is the woman at the well.
John 4 records Jesus speaking with a Samaritan woman whose marital history was complicated.
She had had five husbands, and the man she was then living with was not her husband.
Jesus knew.
He did not need someone to whisper the details to Him.
But notice what the passage does not tell us.
It does not explain how each marriage ended.
It does not say that she caused every separation.
It does not justify labeling her a prostitute.
Those assumptions are often added to the story, but they are not stated by the text.
What Scripture actually shows is even more powerful.
Jesus knew her history and still spoke to her about living water.
He revealed truth without treating her as beyond the reach of God.
And she went back to her community saying:
"Come, see a man, which told me all things that ever I did: is not this the Christ?" (John 4:29, KJV)
The woman who had been fully known became a witness.
The encounter she could not have anticipated became a doorway through which others came to hear Jesus.
Isn't that extraordinary?
The very knowledge that could have made her want to run became part of her testimony.
Because Jesus did not reveal Himself merely to expose her past.
He revealed Himself as the Messiah.
And then there is another woman.
One caught in adultery.
John 7:53–8:11 preserves the famous account of a woman brought before Jesus by religious accusers.

An important textual note belongs here: this passage is absent from many of the earliest Greek manuscripts of John and appears in different locations in some manuscript traditions. Christians should be aware of that textual history rather than conceal it.
The account nevertheless illustrates themes clearly taught elsewhere in Scripture: the danger of hypocritical condemnation, the reality of sin, and the call to turn away from it.
The accusers wanted a spectacle.
Jesus refused to make her humiliation their entertainment.
And in the familiar words of John 8:11, He said:
"Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more." (KJV)
Mercy.
And a command to change.
Neither one canceled the other.
That is the beauty of biblical grace.
Jesus does not need to pretend sin is harmless in order to show mercy to sinners.
And He does not need to humiliate sinners in order to call them to holiness.
But now consider the other side of these stories.
What about the person who did not choose what happened?
What about the girl whose innocence was stolen?
What about the boy who was abused and grew into a man who cannot explain why he feels so much shame?
What about the wife whose husband repeatedly betrayed her?
What about the child caught between two parents who have turned their home into a battlefield?
The Bible does not ignore them.
In 2 Samuel 13, Tamar suffers sexual violence at the hands of her half-brother Amnon.
It is one of Scripture's most heartbreaking accounts.
The text does not present Amnon's violence as love.
It reveals the destruction caused by selfish desire, abuse of power, and injustice.
Tamar protests.
Her suffering matters.
Her voice matters.
And the tragedy is not that she failed to remain pure.
The guilt belongs to the person who violated her.
That is a truth some wounded people desperately need to hear.
What someone did to you is not proof that you are dirty, worthless, or rejected by God.
You do not need to repent for another person's abuse.
You deserve safety, compassion, and appropriate support.
And if someone is currently harming you, seeking protection and help is not a betrayal of faith.
The Lord's compassion is not reserved only for people whose suffering fits neatly into a church testimony.
He sees the wounded.
He sees the betrayed.
He sees the children who learned fear before they learned trust.
He sees the person who still freezes when certain memories return.
And He does not confuse the victim with the offender.
This is why we must read the whole Bible, not merely collect verses that make powerful captions.
Scripture tells the truth about both human sin and human suffering.
It tells us that desire can be beautiful.
It tells us that lust can become destructive.
It tells us that marriage is honorable.
It tells us that families can become places of deep betrayal.
It tells us that people are responsible for their choices.
And it tells us that the wounded must not be crushed beneath the guilt of those who hurt them.
But now we arrive at the moment that changes everything.
Return to Hebrews 4.
Because if we stop at verse 13, we are left standing exposed before a holy God.
Every secret known.
Every motive uncovered.
Every false excuse stripped away.
And the terrifying question becomes:
Who can stand before Him?
Who can survive the truth about themselves?
Who can approach the God who sees what nobody else has seen?
The answer comes immediately.
Hebrews 4:14:
"Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession." (KJV)
There He is.
Jesus.
Not an indifferent observer.
Not a religious celebrity.
Not a Savior who looks away when our stories become uncomfortable.
Our great High Priest.
The One who has entered heaven.
The Son of God.
The One who represents His people before the Father.
And Hebrews continues:
"For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities; but was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin." (Hebrews 4:15, KJV)
That final phrase is everything.
Yet without sin.
Jesus understands human weakness without being guilty of human rebellion.
He knows temptation without surrendering to it.
He knows rejection without becoming cruel.
He knows suffering without becoming corrupt.
He is not merely another broken person telling us to try harder.
He is the sinless Savior who can actually rescue sinners.
The Greek word συμπαθῆσαι (sympathēsai) in Hebrews 4:15 means to sympathize or share in the feeling of another's weakness.
This does not mean Jesus personally committed every sin or experienced every possible human circumstance.
It means His real humanity and sinless endurance make Him a compassionate High Priest who understands the weakness and testing of His people.
And then comes one of the most astonishing invitations in the entire New Testament.
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need." (Hebrews 4:16, KJV)
Wait.
Read that again.
The same passage that says everything is naked and exposed before God tells us to approach His throne with confidence.
How can that be?
Because between our exposure and our invitation stands Jesus Christ.
Our High Priest.
Our mediator.
Our hope.
The Greek expression μετὰ παρρησίας (meta parrēsias) means "with confidence" or "with boldness."
And θρόνῳ τῆς χάριτος (thronō tēs charitos) means "throne of grace."
Not a throne where sin is declared insignificant.
Not a throne where victims are told their suffering does not matter.
Not a throne where repentance is unnecessary.
A throne of grace.
A place where God's mercy is available through Jesus Christ.
And this is the great surprise of Hebrews 4.
The God whose Word exposes everything is the God who invites us to seek mercy through His Son.
You do not have to clean up your entire life before you can cry out to Christ.
You do not have to manufacture a spotless history.
You do not have to convince God that you are better than you really are.
But you must not mistake His invitation for permission to remain comfortably in sin.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come trusting the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
Come ready to surrender what has been ruling you.
And if you have been wounded, come knowing that His mercy is not another accusation against you.
It is an invitation to bring your pain into His care.
Maybe you are reading this after another failure.
You promised you would never open that website again.
But you did.
You promised the affair was over.
But you kept the conversation alive.
You promised you would stop flirting with what was destroying your marriage.
But part of you still wanted the attention.
You promised you would tell the truth.
But the fear of losing your reputation felt stronger than the conviction in your heart.
And now you are exhausted.
Not merely from the sin.
From the hiding.
From pretending.
From living two different lives.
One that people applaud.
And another that keeps you awake at night.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not another secret promise made in a moment of panic.
It is genuine repentance, faith in Jesus Christ, and a willingness to walk in the light.
That may mean confessing what you have hidden.
Ending an immoral relationship.
Seeking pastoral accountability from someone trustworthy.
Getting professional help for compulsive behavior.
Accepting the consequences of your actions.
Making restitution where appropriate.
Or taking the difficult first steps toward rebuilding trust without demanding immediate forgiveness from the people you harmed.
Grace is free to us because of Christ.
But grace is not cheap.
The cross reveals just how seriously God takes sin.
Jesus did not die because our rebellion was harmless.
He died because sin is serious, judgment is real, and humanity cannot save itself.
And the resurrection declares that death does not have the final victory.
This is the Gospel.
Not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
Not shame management.
Not a motivational speech about becoming the best version of yourself.
Jesus Christ came to save sinners, reconcile us to God, and make us new.
And perhaps the most painful thing about your story is that you have begun to believe your worst chapter is your permanent identity.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Failure.
Divorced.
Rejected.
Unwanted.
Damaged.
Unworthy.
Some of those words may describe real choices or circumstances.
But none of them has the authority to replace what God says about those who belong to Christ.
Paul wrote to the Corinthians about people whose former lives had been marked by various sins, including sexual immorality.
Then he said:
"And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God." (1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV)
Such were some of you.
Not because their past never happened.
Not because repentance made consequences disappear.
But because God's saving work had changed their standing and begun changing their lives.
And 2 Corinthians 5:17 announces:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." (KJV)
That does not promise that every relationship will be restored.
It does not guarantee that every marriage will survive betrayal.
It does not mean trauma disappears overnight.
It does not erase legal responsibility or remove the need for patient healing.
But it does mean that through Christ, a person's past need not determine their ultimate future.
And that is why we keep proclaiming this message.
Not because scandal is glamorous.
Not because sin makes a better testimony.
Not because brokenness should be celebrated.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the darkness that brought us to our knees.
He can forgive the guilty.
He can comfort the wounded.
He can humble the proud.
He can strengthen the tempted.
He can restore people who have forgotten what hope feels like.
And He can teach those who have received mercy to become people who extend mercy without compromising truth.
This is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to entertain people with religious controversy.
Not to turn someone's suffering into a spectacle.
But to bring the truth of Scripture into the places where people are silently struggling.
To remind the ashamed that repentance is possible.
To remind the wounded that God has not forgotten them.
To remind families that Christ is worthy of their trust even when life is painfully complicated.
To help believers move beyond inspirational posts into actual discipleship.
Because the world does not need another Christian page that knows how to attract attention but never leads people deeper into the Word.
We need hearts rooted in Scripture.
Minds renewed by truth.
Homes shaped by prayer.
Lives marked by holiness.
And believers who understand that following Jesus is not merely something we do when someone posts a beautiful verse.
It is a daily surrender.
These resources are intended to help believers study the Bible, understand the Gospel, strengthen their prayer lives, grow in spiritual maturity, and remain anchored in Jesus Christ.
And keeping that work going requires real time, effort, resources, and faithful support.
If these messages have helped you return to Scripture, confront a hidden struggle, or remember the mercy of Christ, I want to invite you to consider something beyond reading.
It doesn't.
Not because you owe a monthly payment to prove that you love Jesus.
You don't.
It shouldn't.
But because voluntary, generous support for faithful Gospel ministry can be a meaningful way to honor God and help His Word reach more people.
Scripture teaches that those who receive spiritual instruction may share good things with those who teach (Galatians 6:6), and that giving should be willing rather than compelled (2 Corinthians 9:7).
It is the possibility that another person might encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Someone battling an addiction.
Someone quietly considering abandoning their faith.
Someone sitting alone after discovering their spouse's betrayal.
Someone who believes their sexual past makes them permanently unworthy.
Someone who needs to discover that God calls sinners to repentance and offers mercy through His Son.
You can still help this mission.
Not merely to increase its reach.
Someone may be one honest conversation away from seeking help.
Someone may need to hear that holiness and compassion belong together.
Someone may need to discover that the Bible does not hide from the realities that have shattered their life.
Because there may come a night when the battle feels louder than your prayers.
A night when shame returns.
A night when you need to remember that Hebrews 4 does not end with exposure.
It leads us to Jesus Christ.
And I want to ask you something before you leave.
Not a question designed to make you reveal private details that could endanger you or someone else.
Not an invitation to confess another person's sins publicly.
Just one honest question between your heart and God.
What have you been afraid to bring into the light?
Is it a sin you need to turn away from?
A wound you need help healing?
A marriage that needs truth?
A hidden struggle that needs accountability?
Or a season of exhaustion in which you can barely find the strength to pray?
God already knows.
And the people of God should be a community where truth is spoken with compassion, prayer is offered without spectacle, and struggling people are encouraged to seek wise and trustworthy help.
Before we finish, I want you to imagine something.
Imagine standing before God.
No audience.
No social media profile.
No church title.
No impressive achievements.
No carefully rehearsed explanation.
Everything known.
Every hidden decision.
Every wound.
Every secret.
Every motive.
And imagine understanding, perhaps more clearly than ever before, why you could never save yourself.
Now remember the invitation of Hebrews 4.
There is a great High Priest.
Jesus Christ.
He is holy.
He is sinless.
He is merciful.
He is risen.
And through Him, those who trust in Him may approach the throne of grace.
Not because they have successfully hidden their worst moments.
But because their hope rests in the Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, you can call upon Him today.
A prayer does not save by the mere repetition of its words. Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Christ, and genuine faith turns toward Him in repentance.
But you can speak honestly to Him right now.

"Lord Jesus, You know everything about me. You know my sins, my fears, my wounds, and the things I have tried to hide. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me. Teach me to turn away from sin and follow You. Heal what is wounded, correct what is wrong, and make my life a testimony to Your grace. I surrender myself to You. Amen."
And if you have already trusted Christ but wandered far from Him, hear the call of Scripture again.
Return.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek help where you need it.
Walk in the light.
Do not let shame persuade you that hiding is safer than the mercy of God.
Do not let pride convince you that your reputation matters more than your soul.
And do not let the cruelty of others convince you that Jesus shares their contempt.
The Bible talks about sex because God created human beings as embodied people.
It talks about lust because our desires can become disordered.
It talks about adultery because covenant betrayal matters.
It talks about prostitution because people are more than the sins and circumstances by which society labels them.
It talks about sexual violence because injustice must not be disguised as love.
It talks about broken families because Scripture tells the truth about a fallen world.
And Hebrews 4:12–16 reminds us that the God who knows all these realities also provides a compassionate High Priest.
That is the heart of this message.
Not that God is fascinated by scandal.
But that no scandal is too hidden for His knowledge, no sinner is beyond the reach of His call to repentance, and no wound is beneath His compassion.
The cross does not make evil good.
It reveals the righteousness and mercy of God.
And the empty tomb declares that Jesus Christ is alive.
So stop believing that your only choices are to keep pretending or to give up completely.
There is another way.
The way of truth.
The way of repentance.
The way of grace.
The way of Jesus Christ.

The most frightening thing about coming into the light is discovering that God already knows everything. The most beautiful thing is discovering that, through Jesus Christ, He still invites you to His throne of grace.
